_doc: Single source for SD-39's technology choices (compact cut). Read by video/src/stack.py for the 5.1 technology slides, the stack table, the fix-slide 'Rejected' lines and the C4 technology labels, and by `stack.py sync` for the booklet and OUTLINE.md regions. Slide `how` is two sentences; the rest goes in `detail` (booklet only).

stack.heading: Location index: an in-memory H3 index, sharded by city
stack.title: An in-memory cell index, overwrite-only, owned per city
stack.pick: Go service, H3 resolution 8, in memory
stack.why: A location lives four seconds; all 5 M drivers fit in about 1 GB, so shards are for isolation.
stack.how: Per city: driver → (cell, position, seq) and cell → drivers. Older sequence numbers are dropped; silent drivers expire after 12 s.
stack.detail: H3 resolution 8 cells are about 0.74 km² (edge ≈ 0.46 km); a 2 km search is the k = 2 ring, 19 cells. A cell with more than ~300 drivers is indexed again at resolution 9 so a downtown query reads a few hundred drivers, not thousands. Shards are assigned to cities (big cities split by cell ranges) through a static map in the config service; there are no replicas: a lost shard refills from the next reports within 4 s.
rejected: Members never expire, and every update is a hop to a shared cluster.
A durable write per update: 1.25 M a second of stale data.
stack.course: building-blocks course, part 6 §6.5 (hot keys and hot partitions) and part 17 §17.3 (memory and coordination)
drill: A shard dies with 50,000 drivers on it. What breaks, and for how long?

Matching in that city sees no drivers until they report again: at most one 4 s interval plus reconnect. Nothing durable is lost; the gateway routes updates to the replacement shard, which fills from them.
no replicas; refilled by the next reports within ~4 s

stack.heading: Trip store: PostgreSQL, regional, with conditional claims
stack.title: PostgreSQL: a driver is claimed by one conditional update
stack.why: Claims are thousands a second and must be linearizable: a conditional row update is a compare-and-set.
stack.how: `UPDATE driver_state … WHERE state='available' AND version=$v AND epoch current`. One row back: claimed.
stack.detail: Trips, offers and driver status live here; locations do not. A synchronous standby in another zone means a fail-over cannot forget a claim. The city epoch column fences a deposed matcher leader.
rejected: Asynchronous replication can lose a claim in a fail-over.
A Paxos round per claim, and a second store to run.
summary: a claim is one conditional update
stack.course: building-blocks course, part 8 §8.2 (optimistic concurrency and conditional writes) and part 2 §2.11 (leases and fencing)

stack.heading: Driver gateway: long-lived gRPC streams
stack.title: One stream per driver: locations up, offers down
stack.pick: Go on Kubernetes, gRPC bidirectional streams
stack.why: An open stream delivers an offer in under a second and carries locations too.
stack.how: About 50,000 streams per pod, 100 pods. A driver → pod table lets the matcher push to the right one.
stack.detail: Locations are forwarded to the city's index shard and appended to the location log in batches. A pod drain moves streams gradually with a reconnect hint. Mobile reconnects resume with the last sequence number.
rejected: Offers wait for the next poll.
An honest equal; we already run gRPC.
summary: offers pushed on an open stream

stack.heading: Matcher: one leader per city, behind an etcd lease
stack.title: A single matcher per city, fenced by an epoch
stack.pick: Go service, leader per city via etcd lease
stack.why: One writer per city means no racing matchers; the lease epoch fences a deposed leader.
stack.how: Every 2 s: shortlist 20 per request, one ETA matrix, a min-cost assignment, claims carrying the epoch.
stack.detail: Leases last 5 s; a standby takes over within one lease. The batch window trades up to 2 s of waiting for globally shorter pickups; in quiet cities the tick shortens to 0.5 s.
rejected: An honest equal; a second coordination system.
stack.course: building-blocks course, part 4 §4.3 (leader election) and part 2 §2.11 (fencing tokens)

1: after a fail-over the asynchronous replica may not have it, and the driver is handed out twice.
2: it either leaves riders waiting or takes trips from slow but willing drivers; only a heartbeat lease tells the two apart.
3: neighbours across a prefix boundary share no prefix, and cells distort with latitude.
4: it doubles 1.25 M writes a second to protect data that is stale in four seconds.
5: a river, a one-way street or a highway exit turns 200 m into 12 minutes.
6: it stays green when riders are told “no drivers” while drivers sit idle nearby.
